alphabet.name: kha
alphabet.sound: k with a puff of air after it
alphabet.note: Malayalam pairs almost every consonant with an 'aspirated' twin — same sound, plus a breath. Hold your palm in front of your mouth: ഖ moves it, ക doesn't.

alphabet.name: tha
alphabet.sound: th with the tongue on the teeth, not the roof
alphabet.note: Not the 'th' of 'think'. The tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and the sound is a clean t.

alphabet.name: da
alphabet.sound: d with the tongue on the teeth

alphabet.name: ta
alphabet.sound: t with the tongue curled back
alphabet.note: A 'retroflex' — curl the tongue tip back to the roof of the mouth. English has nothing like it, and mixing it with ത changes words.

alphabet.name: da
alphabet.sound: d with the tongue curled back

alphabet.name: va
alphabet.sound: v, softer than English — closer to w

alphabet.name: zha
alphabet.sound: no English equivalent — tongue curled far back, close to an American r
alphabet.note: The famous one. It appears in the name of the language itself (മലയാളം) and in Kozhikode. If you get ഴ right you sound like you grew up with it.

alphabet.name: na
alphabet.sound: n with the tongue curled back

alphabet.name: la
alphabet.sound: l with the tongue curled back

vocab.note: Malayalam has no plain 'goodbye'. You say 'I'll go and come back' — leaving for good is not what you wish on someone.
Malayalam marks respect by using the plural for one person. 'Nee' to a friend, 'ningal' to anyone older or unfamiliar.
You call your older brother chettan — and also the shopkeeper, the driver, any man a few years older. Using a name alone where chettan belongs sounds abrupt.

examples.translation: My younger brother is at school
Give me a glass of water
What is the price of this?
I need to see a doctor

vocab.note: Malayalam's 'and' attaches to the END of both words rather than sitting between them: chor-um meen-um.

examples.translation: I want to, but I have no money
I didn't come because I was ill
